Transcript Body:
[00:00] Ava: okay hi everyone, thanks for joining, i'm ava from redwood — uh, Redwood Inference, we'll do a quick 45-ish minute runthrough of the sandbox and the playbook for onramp and rescue, and then leave time for q's. Diego's going to demo the console and run a short live stream.
[00:13] Nina: great, thanks, ava, we're excited — we've got a few constraints around latency and PII handling to cover.
[00:17] Tom: yep and i want to understand how the hosted option would fit with our existing VPC and our SSO.
[00:23] Diego: cool, i'll start by sharing my screen, can everyone see the redwood console? (pause) i see yes, ok. so this is the sandbox workspace — it's ephemeral, you can invite engineers, we've preloaded a small dataset and a sample chatflow.
[00:40] Diego: quick note — streaming is chunked every ~300ms by default for this model, you can tune that with chunk_interval on the client side, but the runtime also batches across requests to optimize throughput. sometimes the transcription will say "KV cash" instead of KV cache, you might see that in logs, so just FYI.
[01:05] Nina: when you say batching across requests, does that increase latency for single requests?
[01:10] Diego: good question — we do continuous batching that tries to trade a tiny bit of added headroom wait (usually < 6-8ms) for huge token efficiency. there are low-latency modes you can enable in the runtime for tail-sensitive apps, or pick a small dedicated pool.
[01:25] Sofia: so that's the dedicated vs hosted tradeoff — what would we lose if we stay hosted?
[01:29] Ava: primarily predictability at very high QPS and model pinning; hosted is great for fast start and cost savings, but if you need absolute isolation and fixed latency SLOs, Dedicated or Private gives you GPU pools and reserved capacity. with hosted we offer routing and region pinning and fallbacks.
[01:47] Tom: and how's data handled for hosted? encryption at rest, KMS?
[01:52] Ava: yes — encryption at rest, customer-managed keys via KMS for Private; for hosted we have envelope encryption and can integrate with your key provider for enterprise plans. we'll include the KMS matrix in the security pack.
[02:05] Diego: jumping back — here's a sample chat request in the quickstart. notice the params: temperature 0.2, top_p 0.9, max_tokens 256. those are the obvious knobs. also use stop sequences to limit verbosity rather than strictly relying on max_tokens if you have structured outputs.
[02:25] Diego: streaming behavior: we stream partial tokens as they generate; the client receives deltas. if you have network hiccups, the recommended pattern is to implement at-least-once with idempotency keys on user messages to avoid double billing on retries, and a small exponential backoff.
[02:46] Nina: idempotency keys — is that built into the SDK?
[02:49] Diego: the SDK has helpers for generating and attaching idempotency keys, but you can also use your own request-id header. we generally recommend server-side dedupe so that replays from the client dont create duplicate messages in your conversation state.
[03:05] Tom: what's the typical retry strategy you recommend?
[03:09] Ava: something like: immediate 1st retry for transient network fail, then exponential backoff (200ms, 600ms, 2s) up to 3 attempts, and fallback to cached response if you have prefix caching. but if it's a partial stream you'd handle cleanup on reconnection. we included a retry-playbook in the deck.
[03:30] Diego: i'm going to trigger a live sample: sending a short prompt set from the benchmark sheet. you'll see the stream appear in the console logs and the timeline with latency breakdown. watch the token meter on the right — cost estimate updates in real time.
[03:47] (short pause, typing, demo noise)
[04:10] Diego: okay results — p95 token latency ~120ms, end-to-end 1.1s for this prompt set. that's on the default hosted profile; if we enable a low-latency serving profile we can get p95 under 90ms but cost rises about 18%.
[04:30] Nina: interesting — do you have a calculator for cost vs latency?
[04:34] Ava: yes the Console Optimize tab has a cost/latency heatmap and suggestions — things like quantized model variants, batching windows, or prefix caching recommendations. we'll show you how to run an Optimize audit shortly.
[04:50] Sofia: about compliance — SOC2, audit logs, retention windows?
[04:54] Ava: we keep audit logs per-route, with configurable retention. SOC2 Type II summary is in the security pack; for enterprise we can get you a dedicated audit log sink into your SIEM. retention windows are configurable up to 7 years on Private, hosted has standard tiers — we'll send the exact table.
[05:15] Tom: SSO and RBAC — we use SAML and enforce SCIM provisioning.
[05:19] Ava: yep we support SSO via SAML and OIDC, SCIM provisioning, and role-based access controls at org and route levels. we'll include the SSO setup guide.
[05:34] Diego: quick technical aside — KV cache behavior: long histories are kept in the runtime's KV cache; we also expose cache controls to evict or pin prefixes. sometimes the speech-to-text spits "K-V cash" in notes, haha.
[05:48] (laughter)
[06:00] Nina: about model quality — do you provide eval tooling? we have strict accuracy thresholds for certain intents.
[06:05] Ava: yes, Redwood Optimize includes eval sets and regression alerts; you can tie a prompt set to a quality monitor and get regression emails or webhook alerts when output drift exceeds thresholds.
[06:20] Diego: here's the Optimize audit — it flagged some prompts as high cost because they use long context windows. suggested fixes: prefix caching, reduce max_tokens or offload embeddings for retrieval-augmented generation.
[06:37] Nina: can you demo the retry behavior with a simulated network failure?
[06:40] Diego: yeah i'll throttle my network for a sec. (typing) you can see the client reconnect attempt, we emit a reconnect event and the server will resume streaming; if the request was non-idempotent you'll need your app logic to reconcile duplicates.
[07:05] Tom: what's the recommended pattern for user-visible partial responses? we want to show streaming partials but not commit them until the final token.
[07:11] Diego: render partials as ephemeral UI, mark final when the stream completes; on reconnect you either request missing tail or re-request with idempotency and compare. there's a small UX library in the quickstart that helps with this.
[07:29] Sofia: we're also concerned about embargoed PII — any helper to scrub or automatically redact?
[07:33] Ava: we have pre-built redaction helpers in the SDK and you can run a PII scrub step before sending or after receiving. enterprise plans can opt into on-host redaction pipelines as well.
[07:50] (customer asks about legal/procurement)
[07:55] Nina: timeline — we're aiming for a Q1 pilot. would that be realistic?
[07:59] Ava: absolutely — typical pilot is 2–4 weeks: sandbox onboarding, run benchmarks, tune routing and batching, then a small production pilot. if you're ready we can kick off the pilot on 2026-01-26.
[08:12] Tom: what's the expected ticket for Dedicated vs hosted in early pilot?
[08:16] Ava: pilot cost for hosted is minimal — mostly engineering time; Dedicated requires a reservation but we can do short-term reserved capacity if you need guaranteed throughput. we'll provide a cost estimate after Diego runs the sample workload.
[08:30] Diego: small gotcha: model pinning across rollouts — in hosted we can pin model version per route and run canary rollouts. for strict compliance you might want Private.
[08:45] Nina: okay can you run the full 1k-concurrent run on the sheet now or is that too heavy for the sandbox?
[08:50] Diego: sandbox will throttle, i'd rather run it in a staging pool; i'll schedule it on our staging cluster and post results in the sheet.
[09:00] Diego: i'll note the baseline and then run quantized variant to show cost delta.
[09:08] Ava: and i'll send the security pack right after this call.
[09:12] (customer questions about error codes and observability)
[09:15] Diego: error codes are standard: 429 for over-quota, 503 for capacity, and structured json for model errors. Console tracing shows per-request token breakdown and where the latency is spent (queue, decode, network).
[09:33] Tom: do you expose raw logs or only aggregated metrics?
[09:36] Ava: both— you can stream raw request traces to your log sink for enterprise, plus per-route dashboards in the Console.
[09:45] Nina: do you support per-tenant quotas and token cost caps?
[09:49] Ava: yes, per-route quotas and soft caps; we can configure usage alerts and automated fallbacks to smaller model variants when you hit thresholds.
[10:03] (mid-meeting, fast-forwarded summary of the demo: more parameter examples, Optimize audit, live retry test)
[35:00] Diego: ok jumping to the end, want to highlight a few things: 1) streaming partials + idempotency is the standard pattern for interactive chat 2) use Optimize to find low-cost model variant and caching strategies 3) if you need absolute SLOs use dedicated capacity 4) we'll run your benchmark and share the CSV.
[35:22] Sofia: fine — on action items, can we get a one-pager that maps our 'must-haves' to features?
[35:27] Ava: yes i'll prepare a one-pager and a proposed pilot plan.
[35:32] Tom: procurement concerns — can we get a sample contract and data processing addendum?
[35:37] Ava: absolutely, procurement kit and DPA will be part of the security packet.
[35:45] Nina: last engineering Q: for production, are webhooks for moderation or async callbacks supported?
[35:50] Diego: yes, you can configure webhooks for moderation, asynchronous generation, and post-process hooks.
[36:01] (wrap-up)
[36:10] Ava: ok to recap — next steps: i'll send sandbox invite + quickstart notebook + security pack (SOC2, SSO guide, DPA), diego will run the staging benchmark (1k concurrent) and upload results, nina will share prompt set and traffic pattern, and we'll aim for pilot kickoff on 2026-01-26. any objections?
[36:32] Nina: none, sounds good.
[36:35] Tom: good by me.
[36:37] Sofia: thank you all.
[36:40] Ava: great, we'll follow up in email. thanks for your time.
